title: ZK Proof Systems Lab — Groth16 vs PLONK vs STARK

questions.question: What is a 'trusted setup' in a SNARK proof system?
options: A one-time MPC computation that produces public parameters containing a secret that must be discarded.
A process where the verifier trusts the prover without any cryptographic proof.
A public hash function agreed upon by all parties before proving.
A step where the circuit is compiled into a bytecode format.
questions.explanation: A trusted setup generates a structured reference string (SRS) from a secret 'toxic waste'. Security holds only if at least one participant discards their secret. Anyone who retains it can forge proofs.

questions.question: Why are pairing-based proof systems (Groth16, PLONK) considered not post-quantum safe?
options: They rely on the hardness of discrete logarithm in elliptic curve groups, which Shor's algorithm solves in polynomial time on a quantum computer.
They use SHA-256 which can be broken by Grover's algorithm.
They require a trusted setup, which quantum computers can reverse-engineer.
Their proof sizes are too large for quantum-resistant protocols.
questions.explanation: Groth16 and PLONK security reduces to the discrete logarithm problem in elliptic curve groups. Shor's algorithm solves this in polynomial time on a quantum computer, making these systems insecure in a post-quantum world.

questions.question: Why does Groth16 require a circuit-specific trusted setup while PLONK only requires a universal one?
options: Groth16's SRS encodes the QAP polynomials for one specific circuit; changing any gate requires recomputing the SRS. PLONK encodes only the SRS degree bound and compiles circuit constraints at proof time.
Groth16 uses a larger SRS than PLONK, making it impossible to reuse across circuits.
PLONK does not use a trusted setup at all; it relies purely on hash functions.
Groth16 proofs are smaller, so the setup must be more specific to compensate.
questions.explanation: In Groth16, the setup computes circuit-specific values (QAP evaluations at tau) that are baked into the SRS. PLONK separates the SRS (just powers of tau) from circuit description (selector polynomials), so any circuit up to n_max gates can reuse the same SRS.

questions.question: In the lab, the Groth16 verifier checks A*B ≡ alpha*beta + y*gamma + C*delta (mod p). What does each term represent conceptually?
options: A*B is the prover's work; alpha*beta is the setup binding; y*gamma binds the public input; C*delta is the witness encoding.
A*B is the hash of the witness; alpha*beta is the circuit hash; y*gamma is the output; C*delta is a blinding factor.
All four terms are independent random challenges chosen by the verifier.
A*B encodes the circuit; alpha*beta, y*gamma, C*delta are all public inputs.
questions.explanation: In real Groth16 these are pairing equations: e(A,B) = e(alpha,beta)·e(IC,gamma)·e(C,delta). The alpha*beta term binds the setup, y*gamma binds the public statement, and C*delta binds the proof to the witness. The toy version simulates this with scalar multiplication in F_p.

questions.question: The PLONK proof in this lab has 15 elements (3 wire coms + 1 perm com + 3 quot coms + 6 evaluations + 2 openings). Why are 6 evaluations needed rather than just 3 (one per wire)?
options: PLONK's permutation argument requires evaluations of the permutation polynomial and its selectors at the challenge point, not just the wire values.
PLONK evaluates each wire polynomial at two challenge points for soundness amplification.
The 6 evaluations are needed to verify the 3 multiplication gates separately.
PLONK requires evaluating both the witness and the circuit description polynomials.
questions.explanation: In PLONK, the verifier needs: a(z), b(z), c(z) for the gate identity check, plus s1(z), s2(z) for the permutation argument selectors, plus z(z·ω) for the permutation accumulator at the next point. This totals 6 evaluations.

questions.question: Attack scenario: Alice runs a Groth16 trusted setup ceremony alone and publishes the SRS. Bob wants to use this system. What is the security risk?
options: Alice knows the toxic waste (tau, alpha, beta, gamma, delta) and can forge a proof for any false statement y without knowing a valid witness.
The SRS is too small for circuits with more than 3 gates, so the system is functionally broken.
Bob cannot verify proofs because the verifier key was not published.
The SRS leaks the witness values to anyone who reads it.
questions.explanation: Groth16 security requires at least one participant to have deleted their secret. If Alice alone ran the ceremony and kept tau, she can solve for C in A*B = alpha*beta + y_fake*gamma + C*delta for any fake y, forging a valid-looking proof. This is why real ceremonies involve hundreds of independent participants.

questions.question: A STARK proof in this lab has 11 hash values (roots + query responses). Why does STARK proof size grow as O(log²n) rather than O(log n)?
options: Each of the O(log n) FRI layers requires O(log n) Merkle authentication path hashes per query, so total hashes are O(log n × log n).
STARK uses two independent hash functions, doubling the proof size compared to a single-hash scheme.
The constraint polynomial has degree n², requiring twice as many FRI folding rounds.
STARK repeats the FRI protocol log n times for soundness amplification.
questions.explanation: FRI has O(log n) folding layers. At each layer, opening a query requires an O(log n)-deep Merkle path. With O(security_param) queries, total cost is O(security_param × log²n). The security parameter is typically 80–128 bits, making STARK proofs significantly larger than SNARKs for practical circuit sizes.

questions.question: You are building a ZK rollup that must verify proofs on Ethereum (expensive gas), use circuits that change monthly, and support post-quantum migration in 5 years. Which system fits best today and why?
options: PLONK: universal setup avoids monthly ceremonies, proof size is acceptable on-chain, and it can be replaced with a hash-based variant (e.g., Plonky2) when PQ migration is needed.
Groth16: smallest proof minimises gas, and the monthly ceremony is a minor inconvenience.
STARK: post-quantum safe now and no setup required, so it satisfies all three constraints immediately.
None: no single system satisfies all three constraints simultaneously.
questions.explanation: PLONK's universal setup avoids a new ceremony each month (ruling out Groth16). Its ~15-element proof is manageable on-chain (STARKs have much larger proofs, costing more gas). The PQ migration path exists via FRI-based PLONK variants (Plonky2, Halo2 with IPA). STARK's larger proof size would make on-chain verification significantly more expensive today.
